📋 Overview

📚
References: Tintinalli 9th Ch.260 · ATLS 11th (Airway Ch.4 + Secondary Survey Ch.14) · Rosen's 10th

Neck trauma is divided into penetrating and blunt. Emergency management focuses on identifying vascular, airway, and esophageal injuries rapidly. The 3-zone anatomic system guides surgical approach and diagnostic workup.

🔴
Critical priorities: Airway first (may be distorted/compromised). Hemorrhage control. Distinguish hard vs soft signs to decide: OR immediately vs MDCTA workup.
🎯 Examiner mindset: Two key concepts that appear every exam cycle: (1) Hard vs soft signs — hard → OR, soft → MDCTA. (2) Zone anatomy — zone I needs thoracic exposure, zone II is most common and accessible.

📖 ATLS 11th — Neck Zones Reference

📚
Source: ATLS 11th Edition, Chapter 22: Penetrating Trauma — Table 22-1: Zones of the Neck

Zone I (below cricoid → thoracic outlet): surgical access may require thoracotomy/sternotomy. Zone II (cricoid → angle of mandible): most common zone; access via standard neck incision. Zone III (above angle of mandible → skull base): distal control is very difficult; endovascular approach preferred.

📖 Rosen's EM 10th — Neck Zones Anatomy

📚
Source: Rosen's Emergency Medicine 10th Edition, Chapter 36: Neck Trauma — Fig. 36.1: Zones of the Neck

The no-zone approach for stable patients: MDCTA evaluates all three zones simultaneously with 98-100% NPV, replacing zone-based mandatory exploration. Hard signs override zone classification — immediate OR regardless of zone.

🫀 Neck Anatomy & Zones

Zone I — Below Cricoid

Cricoid cartilage → clavicle / sternal notch (thoracic outlet)

⚠️ Proximal vascular control requires sternotomy or thoracotomy — surgically most difficult

Contents: Common carotid artery origin, subclavian vessels, vertebral artery origin, trachea, esophagus, thoracic duct, brachial plexus, apex of lung

Penetrating: most patients with Zone I/III injuries historically underwent angiography + endoscopy to determine need for operative intervention

Zone II — Midneck ✓ Most Common Injury

Cricoid cartilage → angle of mandible

✅ Most commonly injured zone; most surgically accessible via standard neck incision

Historical mandatory exploration began WWII — now REPLACED by selective MDCTA-guided management to minimize negative explorations

Contents: Common carotid, internal/external carotid, vertebral artery, internal jugular vein, larynx, trachea, esophagus, vagus nerve

Zone III — Above Angle of Mandible

Angle of mandible → base of skull

⚠️ Distal control near skull base is technically challenging; endovascular approach (embolization or stenting) preferred over open surgery

Contents: Distal internal carotid, vertebral arteries, jugular vein, cranial nerves IX–XII

⚡
Key landmark — Platysma muscle: Wounds NOT violating platysma = superficial → local wound care and discharge if stable, no further workup needed. Wounds violating platysma = potentially significant → requires evaluation (MDCTA ± endoscopy based on clinical signs).

Neck Anatomy — Textbook Figures

🎯 Examiner mindset: Zone I = thoracic approach for proximal control. Zone II = most common + most accessible. Zone III = skull base difficulty with distal control. The platysma rule is a classic single-best-answer exam scenario.

🔪 Penetrating Neck Trauma

🔥 ออกสอบบ่อย

Penetrating neck trauma composes the majority of traumatic neck injuries. Management hinges on two key questions: (1) Does the wound violate the platysma? (2) Are hard or soft signs present?

Hard vs Soft Signs of Significant Injury

🔴
HARD Signs → OR or Interventional Angio Immediately
(Do NOT delay for CT)
  • Active arterial hemorrhage
  • Expanding or pulsatile hematoma
  • Airway compromise (stridor, obstruction)
  • Neurologic deficit (hemiplegia, focal deficit)
  • Absent radial pulse
  • Air bubbling from wound
  • Massive subcutaneous emphysema

The overwhelming majority of patients with hard signs of vascular injury will require operative intervention (Tintinalli)

🟡
SOFT Signs → MDCTA Workup
(Stable patient; up to 25% have vascular abnormality, but only 3% need repair)
  • Hoarseness, voice change
  • Mild dysphagia
  • Non-expanding hematoma
  • Subcutaneous emphysema (mild)
  • Hemoptysis, hematemesis
  • Bruit or thrill over vessel
  • Wound near vital structures
🔥 ออกสอบบ่อย

Q: Which of the following is a HARD sign of significant penetrating neck injury requiring immediate OR?

Evolution of Management: Mandatory → Selective → No-Zone Approach

1. Mandatory Operative Exploration (Historical)

Historically, ALL Zone II injuries were surgically explored — a practice that began during World War II in response to high incidence of missed injuries and mortality. However, this aggressive approach leads to high rates of negative explorations. Zone II is the most commonly injured zone and is easily accessed surgically; exposure and vascular control are more difficult for Zone I and III.

2. Selective Management

Movement toward selective management began in response to high rates of negative neck explorations. Selective protocols mandate rapidly obtained angiography, esophagography, and panendoscopy for symptomatic patients, with observation alone for asymptomatic patients. These approaches have radically decreased nontherapeutic neck operations without increasing morbidity and mortality. However, the yield of angiography and endoscopy in asymptomatic patients is exceedingly low.

3. No-Zone Targeted Diagnostic Workup (Current Best Practice)

A new iteration in selective management has evolved with the addition of MDCTA. MDCTA now permits fast, reliable information about injuries in all neck zones. Per this protocol, the zone of injury has little impact on management — the neck is considered a single unit.

  • Symptomatic patients with hard signs → emergent operative or angiographic intervention
  • Symptomatic patients with soft signs → MDCTA; further diagnostic testing guided by MDCTA findings
  • Symptomatic patients with indeterminate MDCTA artifact → traditional testing (angiography + endoscopy)
  • Asymptomatic patients → can be observed with serial exams at high-volume centers

MDCTA — Primary Diagnostic Tool

  • Physical exam + MDCTA: 100% sensitive, 97.5% specific for significant vascular/aerodigestive injury
  • NPV for arterial injury: 98–100% — justifies selective management
  • Evaluates all 3 zones simultaneously: vascular + aerodigestive tracts + cervical spine + osseous structures
  • Defines wound trajectory → low-risk trajectory = no further invasive workup needed; high-risk trajectory near vital structures = targeted workup
  • <2% of MDCTAs are nondiagnostic due to artifact (metallic foreign bodies, motion)
  • Disadvantages: ionizing radiation, iodinated contrast, image artifacts, post-MDCTA angiography may pose unnecessary contrast nephropathy risk (though incidence lower than previously believed)

Other Imaging Modalities

  • Color flow Doppler US: Highly sensitive for clinically important vascular injuries. Advantages: portable, noninvasive, no radiation, lower cost. Disadvantages: cannot penetrate bone (no Zone I/III evaluation), operator-dependent variability, cannot evaluate aerodigestive tract, limited by subcutaneous emphysema/hematoma
  • Catheter angiography: Gold standard (diagnostic + therapeutic). Can provide definitive endovascular repair. Disadvantages: invasive, expensive, labor-intensive, requires skilled operators, limited availability, cannot evaluate aerodigestive structures
  • MRI/MRA: Contraindicated with metallic projectiles (ferromagnetic). Variable sensitivity (50–100%) for BCVI; role not fully evaluated for aerodigestive injuries. Use only if absolute contraindication to iodinated contrast
⚡ ออกสอบปานกลาง

Q: What is the negative predictive value (NPV) of MDCTA for arterial injury in penetrating neck trauma?

🎯 Examiner mindset: The shift from mandatory → selective Zone II exploration is the highest-yield concept. NPV 98–100% is the statistical justification. Know the no-zone approach: it treats the neck as a SINGLE UNIT regardless of zone.

🩸 Penetrating Vascular Injuries

🔥 ออกสอบบ่อย

Vascular injuries are present in up to 40% of penetrating neck trauma and are the most commonly associated cervical injury in this population.

Epidemiology

  • Arterial injuries account for 45% of penetrating neck vascular trauma — most frequent cause of death
  • Predominantly involves the carotid artery
  • Carotid artery injury → stroke in 15%, death in up to 22%
  • Venous injuries discovered in up to 20% of penetrating neck wounds; signs often subtle and difficult to identify by physical exam
  • Most asymptomatic venous injuries do not require repair
  • Up to one quarter of patients with soft signs of vascular injury will have a vascular abnormality at angiography, but only 3% of these patients will require vascular repair

Treatment Options

Treatment depends on the vessel involved and accessibility of the lesion. Options range from observation to surgical repair to angiographic embolization or stenting.

  • Asymptomatic carotid artery injuries, low-velocity wounds, small intimal tears or pseudoaneurysms: may NOT need repair if intact distal circulation and reliable surgical follow-up
  • Stable patients with injuries suitable for endovascular repair may undergo definitive angiographic intervention at time of catheter angiography
  • Angiography findings inconclusive or incongruent with clinical exam → refine with digital subtraction angiography
ℹ️
Catheter angiography: Remains gold standard for penetrating neck vascular injuries. Provides diagnostic AND therapeutic capability (embolization, stenting). Access to Zone I and III injuries where surgical repair is difficult. Disadvantages: invasive, expensive, labor-intensive, limited availability, potential complications (nephropathy, puncture site hematoma, thrombosis, embolism, vascular spasm, ischemia, arterial dissection).

🧠 Blunt Cerebrovascular Injury (BCVI)

⚡ ออกสอบปานกลาง

Blunt neck trauma composes only 5% of traumatic injuries to the neck. Road traffic accidents are the most common cause; other causes include assault, pedestrians struck by vehicles, falls, and hanging.

Vascular injury occurs in approximately 1% of patients with blunt neck trauma. Most patients with BCVI are initially asymptomatic — symptoms (TIA, stroke) may develop hours to days later. The mortality rate of symptomatic BCVI approaches 60%.

Why Screen?

  • Angiographic screening of certain asymptomatic patients can increase the likelihood of diagnosis 10-fold
  • Early identification and treatment of BCVI significantly reduces stroke and death rates
  • Using traditional criteria, 20% of BCVIs occur without any established risk factor
  • An estimated 96% of trauma patients would need to be screened to capture all injuries — so expanded Denver criteria are used to target highest-risk patients
  • An expanded Denver screening protocol is purported to reduce missed BCVIs to 5%

Mechanism of Blunt Cerebrovascular Injury

The mechanism is cervical hyperextension and rotation, or hyperextension during rapid deceleration. This can result in intimal tears, dissections, pseudoaneurysms, fistulas, and intimal flaps in the carotid and vertebral arteries. The adventitia of vessels in blunt trauma injuries is composed largely of inelastic collagen that acts as a substrate for thromboembolism.

⚡ ออกสอบปานกลาง

Q: Which fracture pattern should prompt screening for blunt cerebrovascular injury (BCVI)?

Denver Screening Criteria (Table 260-7)

BCVI Grading Scale (Table 260-8)

Diagnosis

  • MDCTA: Initial screening modality of choice. NPV approaching 100% for subsequent stroke. However, false-positive rate of approximately 45% — confirm true positives with digital subtraction angiography before committing to anticoagulation
  • Catheter angiography (digital subtraction): Confirm positive MDCTA; continue anticoagulation until results confirm need for further therapy
  • Color Doppler US: Should NOT be used as a screening test for BCVI (insufficient sensitivity for Zones I and III)
  • MRI: Variable sensitivity (50–100%) and specificity (29–100%) vs digital subtraction angiography; do not use as sole screening study unless absolute contraindication to iodinated contrast

Treatment

Patients with untreated or undiagnosed BCVI have up to 60% risk for stroke, with rates increasing with injury grade severity.

  • Antithrombotic agents (aspirin, clopidogrel, or heparin) dramatically reduce mortality and morbidity — treatment of choice for most grades
  • No significant differences in outcomes between anticoagulant vs antiplatelet therapy demonstrated
  • Antithrombotic agents are safe even in patients with traumatic brain injury, solid organ injury, spinal cord injury, or concomitant neurologic hemorrhage
  • Specific therapy determined by grading scale (Table 260-8): Grades I–IV = antithrombotic ± surgical repair; Grade V = surgical repair if accessible or balloon occlusion/embolization
⚠️
Airway is the priority in blunt neck trauma: Airway occlusion rather than hemorrhage is the most rapidly fatal injury in blunt neck trauma (vs penetrating where hemorrhage dominates).
🎯 Examiner mindset: Know Denver criteria by heart. MDCTA false-positive rate 45% → confirm with DSA. 60% stroke risk untreated. Antithrombotics safe even with TBI. Horner syndrome = screen for BCVI.

💨 Airway & Esophageal Injuries

Laryngotracheal Injuries

⚡ ออกสอบปานกลาง

Penetrating neck trauma causes laryngotracheal injury in 2% to 5% of penetrating trauma patients with a 2% to 15% mortality rate. Blunt laryngotracheal injuries occur in less than 0.5% of blunt trauma patients (usually car collisions).

Why Blunt Laryngotracheal Injuries Are Rare

The larynx is protected by the mandible and supported by muscles that deflect most external forces. However, patients with blunt laryngotracheal injuries may have a quiescent phase with progressively increasing subclinical airway edema or hematoma that can result in delayed airway obstruction — making early recognition critical.

Assessment

Significant laryngotracheal injuries should be detected by physical exam. Patients with hard signs of laryngotracheal injury need urgent airway control and operative intervention. Soft signs of laryngotracheal injury are present in approximately 18% of patients with penetrating neck injury, but only 15% of these patients will have a laryngotracheal injury diagnosed.

Airway Management Indications — Textbook Tables

🔴
Laryngeal Injury Grade → Management:
  • Grade I (hematoma, no fracture): Observation, voice rest, head-of-bed elevation
  • Grade II (edema/hematoma, nondisplaced fracture, no exposed cartilage): Observation ± microlaryngoscopy
  • Grade III (exposed cartilage, displaced fracture, vocal fold immobility): Surgical intervention required
  • Grade IV (Grade III + 2+ fracture lines or massive mucosal trauma): Surgical intervention required
  • Grade V (complete laryngotracheal separation): Emergent surgical repair — often requires intubation through tracheal defect
📌 ออกสอบน้อย

Q: A patient has laryngeal edema, hematoma, and a nondisplaced fracture without exposed cartilage. Laryngeal injury grade?

Esophageal / Pharyngoesophageal Injuries

Penetrating Esophageal Injuries

  • Evaluation: esophagoscopy or esophagram (combined esophagram + esophagoscopy has 100% sensitivity)
  • Perforations >2 cm and esophageal perforations → surgical repair
  • Small perforations or undisplaced tears: IV antibiotics for 7–10 days, nasogastric or total parenteral nutrition, ± operative repair or conservative management
  • Morbidity and mortality primarily from delayed diagnosis → mediastinitis and sepsis

Blunt Pharyngoesophageal Injuries

  • Exceedingly rare: Only 11 cases of cervical digestive tract injury due to blunt forces reported between 1970 and 2003
  • Mechanism: esophagus forced against the spine during sudden acceleration/deceleration with neck extension
  • Low incidence + subtle clinical presentation → delay in diagnosis → morbidity and mortality
  • Signs/symptoms of pharyngoesophageal injury from blunt trauma are much more likely to result from laryngotracheal pathology — making diagnosis challenging
  • Radiography, CT, and MRI can provide detailed information on soft tissue neck structures
🎯 Examiner mindset: Laryngeal grading threshold: Grade III = exposed cartilage = operative intervention. Blunt laryngotracheal injuries are rare but have a quiescent phase — delay in airway compromise is the classic teaching point.

⚠️ Strangulation

⚡ ออกสอบปานกลาง

Strangulation is one form of blunt neck trauma. 10% of violent deaths in the United States are due to strangulation. Hanging is the second most common means of suicide death in the United States.

Mechanisms

  • Hanging (judicial, suicidal, accidental)
  • Postural strangulation
  • Ligature strangulation
  • Manual (homicidal) strangulation
  • Accidental strangulation in children (clothing/hair entangled in machinery) or adults (erotic asphyxiation)

Pathophysiology — Why Venous Obstruction, Not Airway

Although airway compromise is widely envisioned as the cause of strangulation deaths, the major pathologic mechanism is obstruction of cerebral venous return. Evidence: case reports of people with functioning tracheostomies committing suicide by hanging/strangulation — demonstrating death is possible even with a patent airway.

Pathophysiologic sequence:

  1. Venous compression: Only limited pressure needed; if both external and internal jugular veins are simultaneously occluded → cerebral vascular congestion, edema, and unconsciousness
  2. Loss of muscle tone: Allows arterial compression → subsequent cerebral anoxia
  3. Minor mechanisms: Airway obstruction, carotid body reflex-mediated cardiac dysrhythmia
⚡
KEY: 50% of strangulation victims have no visible signs of neck trauma. Two-thirds are asymptomatic. Patients with extensive laryngeal injury may have few external signs.

Associated Injuries

  • Laryngotracheal fractures
  • Cervical spine fractures (rare except in judicial hanging with a drop)
  • Pharyngeal lacerations
  • Carotid artery injuries / dissection
  • Hyoid bone fracture: Classically associated with strangulation but found in a minority of cases — even those with fatal injuries. Not a reliable diagnostic sign.
  • Cervical spine + cord injuries: not frequently seen in survivors (mainly in judicial hangings)

Clinical Features

  • Petechiae (especially conjunctival), neck contusions — present in only ~50% of victims
  • Two-thirds of victims are asymptomatic at presentation
  • Symptoms when present: neck pain, voice changes, swallowing difficulty, breathing problems — any can signal impending airway compromise
  • Prognosis: Patients in cardiac arrest have a dismal prognosis. Neurologic recovery is unpredictable — patients with GCS 3 may recover without sequelae, while those with normal initial exams may progressively deteriorate
  • Most in-hospital poststrangulation deaths occur due to laryngeal or pulmonary edema or cerebral anoxia
  • Delayed fatality risk: A subset of seemingly asymptomatic patients may die after developing delayed cerebral or pulmonary edema

Diagnosis & Management

  • Patients with hard signs of vascular or laryngotracheal injuries → intraoperative endoscopy if pharyngoesophageal injury suspected
  • Carotid artery imaging to exclude carotid dissection — indicated even in asymptomatic patients
  • Consider unreported strangulation in young patients with acute neurologic deficits or spontaneous carotid artery dissection
  • CT/MRI: Provides detailed information of soft tissue structures. Radiologic signs: intramuscular hemorrhage/edema, swelling of platysma, subcutaneous bleeding, hemorrhagic lymph nodes
  • Difficult clinical scenario: "Walking and talking" victim without physical signs; may be under influence of alcohol/drugs or hyperventilating; physicians may be tempted to ascribe symptoms to anxiety
⚡ ออกสอบปานกลาง

Q: What percentage of strangulation victims have NO visible signs of neck trauma?

🎯 Examiner mindset: Classic exam trap: absent external signs does NOT exclude serious strangulation injury. Death mechanism = venous obstruction (not airway). Hyoid fracture is associated but NOT required for diagnosis. Always image carotids even if asymptomatic.

⭐ Key Points — Ch.260 Neck Trauma

  1. Platysma = key landmark: non-violating wound → local care; violating → workup
  2. Zone I (below cricoid→thoracic outlet): proximal control requires sternotomy
  3. Zone II (cricoid→angle of mandible): most common, most accessible; mandatory exploration now replaced by selective MDCTA-guided management
  4. Zone III (above angle→skull base): distal control difficult; endovascular preferred
  5. Hard signs → OR immediately (no CT first): active hemorrhage, expanding hematoma, airway compromise, neuro deficit
  6. Soft signs → MDCTA (NPV 98–100%; evaluates all zones + aerodigestive + spine)
  7. BCVI: screen with Denver criteria; grade I–V; treat with antithrombotic agents
  8. Horner syndrome = Denver BCVI criterion → carotid dissection until proven otherwise
  9. Strangulation: 50% no visible signs; death from cerebral venous obstruction; image carotids
  10. Laryngeal Grade III+ (exposed cartilage) = surgical intervention threshold
